entries.title: Why are so many Thai restaurants hidden in London pubs?

fields.author: Mei Lin
fields.standfirst: Behind the bar of a hundred old pubs, a small kitchen turns out some of the city’s best green curry. How a licensing quirk of the 1980s built a tradition.
fields.image_alt: A pub kitchen hatch with a handwritten Thai menu above it
fields.body:
Walk into an old pub in London and there is a good chance the kitchen at the back is Thai. There are more than a hundred of them, and most began the same way.

In the 1980s, landlords who had lost their food trade could let their kitchens to a cook without a second licence. Thai families, many newly arrived, took them on, and the arrangement stuck.

Our travel writer spent a week eating her way round twelve of them. The best green curry, she reports, was served under a dartboard.

entries.title: A walk along the old railway line before it becomes a road

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Nine miles of cuttings, bridges and one surprised heron.
fields.image_alt: An overgrown railway cutting with a stone bridge in the distance
fields.body:
The branch line closed in 1965. Next spring the county starts building a relief road along it, so we walked the whole nine miles while we still can.

There are four stone bridges, a tunnel the bats have claimed, and a cutting so deep it keeps its frost until noon. The platform at Low End is still there under the brambles.

The county says a footpath will run beside the new road. It will not, we suspect, have the heron.

entries.title: The allotment waiting list is now eleven years long

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: Why plots stay empty while the list grows, and what the council plans.
fields.image_alt: Allotment plots with sheds and bean poles under a grey sky
fields.body:
There are 214 names on the waiting list for the town’s 96 allotment plots. At the current rate of turnover, the last name on it will get a plot in 2037.

Yet on a walk around the site this week we counted eleven plots that had not been worked this year. The council says tenants have until the spring inspection to bring them back into use, and it plans to halve the size of new plots so more people get one.
fields.key_facts:
Plots: 96
Names on the list: 214
Plots unworked this year: 11

entries.title: What a year of tracking every bus in the valley taught us

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: The 7:40 is late on 62 per cent of days. The 7:55 almost never is.
fields.image_alt: A bus pulling away from a stop on the high street
fields.body:
For a year we logged the arrival of every bus at the four stops on the high street: 21,000 arrivals in all, recorded by readers, a newsagent and one very patient retired teacher.

The 7:40 to the station is late on 62 per cent of days, by four minutes on average. The 7:55, which leaves the depot rather than coming over the ridge, is late on fewer than one day in twenty.

The bus company says it will move the 7:40’s start point from next spring. Until then, our advice is the 7:55.
fields.key_facts:
Arrivals logged: 21,000
The 7:40 late: 62 per cent of days
The 7:55 late: 4 per cent of days

entries.title: Inside the bakery that has opened at 4am every day since 1958

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: Two ovens, one family and a queue that starts before the first bus.
fields.image_alt: Loaves cooling on wooden racks in a bakery before dawn
fields.body:
The lights at Hollins Bakery come on at a quarter to four. By the time the first bus passes at six, there are three hundred loaves on the racks and a queue at the door.

The bakery has opened at four every day since Albert Hollins took over the lease in 1958, Christmas Day included. His granddaughter Jo runs it now, on the same two ovens he installed.

Asked why they have never moved the opening time, Jo Hollins said the night shift at the mill finishes at four. “They were our first customers. They still are.”

entries.title: The last lighthouse keeper on the east coast hands over the keys

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Forty-one years, three storms that made the news and one that did not.
fields.image_alt: The white lighthouse on the point, waves breaking below it
fields.body:
Ellen Marsh climbed the 114 steps of the point lighthouse for the last time on Tuesday morning. The light has been automatic since 1998, but someone still had to keep it, and for forty-one years that was her.

She remembers three storms that made the national news, and one in 1987 that did not, when the lamp failed at two in the morning and she turned it by hand until dawn.

The keys go to the trust that now owns the tower. Marsh is moving to a bungalow inland. “I want to sleep through a gale,” she said.

entries.title: 12 of the best films to watch in November

fields.author: Sam Okafor
fields.standfirst: From the festival winner opening at the old Regal to two reissues worth the drive, the films to see before the year turns.
fields.image_alt: Rows of red seats in the old Regal cinema
fields.body:
The Regal opens this year’s festival winner on the 14th, a quiet film about a lock keeper that won the audience prize as well as the jury’s.

Two restorations are worth the drive to the city: a 1950s thriller with a new score, and a documentary about the last steam trains, shot partly on our own branch line.

entries.title: 12 of the best TV shows to watch this November

fields.author: Ana Ruiz
fields.standfirst: A heist in the fog, a slow-burn courtroom drama and the comedy everyone at the office is quoting. Our critics pick the month.
fields.image_alt: The lit marquee of the old Regal cinema at night
fields.body:
November is the month the schedules fill up. Our critics have watched the first episodes so you do not have to, and picked the twelve worth your evenings.

At the top of the list is a six-part heist set on a fog-bound island, followed by a courtroom drama that takes three episodes to get going and is worth every minute of them.

entries.title: What the forecast got wrong this week

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Tuesday was meant to be dry. The valley got eleven millimetres. Why the national models keep missing the rain that arrives at four.
fields.image_alt: Storm clouds gathering over the ridge in the afternoon
fields.body:
The national forecast for Tuesday promised a dry day with sunny spells. The gauge at the mill bridge collected eleven millimetres, most of it between four and half past.

Forecasters say the national models work on a grid too coarse to see a valley this narrow. Our own record suggests a simpler rule: if the morning is warm and still, take a coat at four.

entries.title: River levels, and what the gauge at the bridge means

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: The painted scale on the mill bridge pier is read by half the valley. Here is what each mark means, and when to move the car.
fields.image_alt: The painted depth scale on a stone bridge pier
fields.body:
The white scale painted on the mill bridge pier is the most-read measuring instrument in the valley. It runs from 0 to 3 metres, and the river sits between 0.6 and 0.9 for most of the year.

At 1.5 metres the meadow path floods. At 2 metres the council closes the riverside car park, and at 2.4 the water reaches the cellars on Mill Lane. The highest mark, from 1968, is cut into the stone at 2.9.
fields.key_facts:
Normal level: 0.6 to 0.9 metres
Meadow path floods: 1.5 metres
Car park closes: 2 metres
Record, 1968: 2.9 metres

entries.title: Fog season begins two weeks early

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Three foggy mornings this week, the earliest run since records began at the school weather station. Expect more until the wind turns.
fields.image_alt: Fog filling the valley below the town at first light
fields.body:
The valley woke to fog on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday this week, the earliest run of fog mornings since the school weather station began keeping records in 1998.

Clear nights and still air let the cold sink to the valley floor. Forecasters expect more of the same until the wind turns westerly early next week. Drivers on the ridge road are asked to use dipped headlights until ten.

entries.title: We should take the sign down ourselves

fields.author: The editors
fields.standfirst: The rusted sign above the town has been “awaiting removal” for four years. A Saturday morning and a few spanners would do it.
fields.image_alt: A leaning, rusted sign on the ridge road above the town
fields.body:
The welcome sign on the ridge road has leaned a little further every winter since 2022. It has been on the council’s list for removal for four years, behind a dispute over who owns the verge it stands on.

We think the town should stop waiting. A dozen volunteers, a van and a Saturday morning would do it, and the parish council has offered to store the sign until someone decides what to do with it.

entries.title: Bus driver’s first novel sells out at the station kiosk

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Dennis Hale wrote it between shifts on the 14. The kiosk ordered forty copies and sold the last one before lunch on Wednesday.
fields.image_alt: The bus station at the top of the high street
fields.body:
Dennis Hale has driven the number 14 for nineteen years. He wrote most of his first novel in the layover at the top of the valley, in a notebook on the steering wheel.

The station kiosk took forty copies on Monday and had none left by Wednesday lunchtime. Another sixty arrive on Saturday. “People ask me to sign them at the bus stop,” Hale said. “I tell them I have a timetable to keep.”

entries.title: Council votes tonight on the closed path above the town

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: The ridge path has been fenced off since a landslip in March. Councillors choose tonight between a £180,000 repair and a permanent diversion.
fields.image_alt: The town from the ridge, roofs and the church spire in the mist
fields.body:
The footpath along the ridge above the town has been closed since a landslip in March took out forty metres of it. Tonight the council decides whether to rebuild it or route walkers through the woods below for good.

Engineers put the repair at £180,000. The diversion would cost a tenth of that, but adds a mile and loses the view over the valley that most people walk the path for.

More than 900 people have signed a petition to reopen it. The meeting starts at seven in the town hall and is open to the public.
fields.key_facts:
Length of path lost: 40 metres
Cost to repair: £180,000
Petition signatures: 912

entries.title: Valley rain arrives at four, study confirms

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: A six-year study finds the afternoon showers are as regular as residents have always claimed, and more so in October.
fields.image_alt: A rain gauge on the rail of the mill bridge, the river high below it
fields.body:
The showers begin, on average, at 4:07 in the afternoon and last twenty-two minutes. The study, which logged every rainfall in the valley since 2020, found the pattern held on most days from May to October.

It held on 71 per cent of days between May and October, and on almost every day in the first two weeks of October, when the warm valley floor meets the first cold air off the ridge.

Residents at the mill bridge say they have planned their walks around it for years. The authors now want to know why October is the most punctual month of all, and they will keep the gauge running through next spring.
fields.image_credit: The gauge at the mill bridge, Thursday afternoon. Photo: Tom Reilly
fields.key_facts:
Days with afternoon rain, May to October: 71 per cent
Average shower: 22 minutes
Median start: 4:07 in the afternoon

entries.title: The one café raises prices for the first time in nine years

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: A pot of tea goes from £1.80 to £2.20 on Monday. The owners say flour, milk and the electricity bill left them no choice.
fields.image_alt: The café on the high street, its windows steamed up
fields.body:
The Bridge Café, the only café in the valley, is raising its prices on Monday for the first time since 2017. A pot of tea goes from £1.80 to £2.20, and a bacon roll from £3 to £3.60.

“We held out as long as we could,” said Ruth Aske, who has run it with her brother since their mother retired. Flour has doubled in price in two years, and the electricity bill for the ovens is now their largest cost after wages.

Regulars at the window table on Thursday took the news calmly. Most said they would keep coming. One said he would bring his own biscuits.

entries.title: Library extends its Sunday hours through the winter

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: From November the library opens from ten until four on Sundays, two hours longer, paid for by the council’s warm-spaces fund.
fields.body:
The library on Church Street will open from ten until four on Sundays from 2 November until the end of March, two hours longer than now.

The extra hours come from the council’s warm-spaces fund. The reading room keeps its heating on all day, and the urn in the corner will be filled.

entries.title: Reservoir at 82 per cent after a wet October

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: The highest October level in six years, up from 64 per cent at the start of the month. The hosepipe ban is formally lifted.
fields.body:
The valley reservoir stood at 82 per cent this morning, its highest October reading since 2020 and up from 64 per cent on the first of the month.

The water company has formally lifted the hosepipe ban it imposed in July. It says levels would need to fall below 55 per cent before it considered another.
fields.key_facts:
Level this morning: 82 per cent
On 1 October: 64 per cent
Hosepipe ban threshold: 55 per cent

entries.title: Market stalls return to the square on Saturday

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Twenty-two traders have signed up for the first market since the square was resurfaced, from the cheese van to a new coffee cart.
fields.body:
The Saturday market returns to the square this weekend for the first time since resurfacing began in August. Twenty-two traders have booked pitches, four of them new.

Stalls open at eight and close at two. Parking on the square itself stays suspended until the new lines are painted, so the council asks shoppers to use the station car park.

entries.title: School board sets the new term dates

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: The spring term starts on 5 January, a day later than last year, and half term moves to the third week of February.
fields.body:
The valley school board has fixed next year’s term dates. The spring term starts on Tuesday 5 January, a day later than last year, so staff can use the Monday for training.

Half term moves to the week of 15 February to line up with the two neighbouring districts, which the board says will help families with children at more than one school.

entries.title: Road closed at the mill bridge after a lorry sheds its load

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Mill Bridge Road is shut in both directions while the council clears forty tonnes of gravel. Buses are running via Station Lane.
fields.body:
Mill Bridge Road is closed in both directions after a lorry shed its load of gravel on the approach to the bridge shortly after nine this morning. No one was hurt.

Council crews expect to reopen one lane by mid-afternoon. The 14 and 22 buses are running via Station Lane until then, and the footbridge stays open.

fields.body:
For a year we logged the arrival of every bus at the four stops on the high street: 21,000 arrivals in all, recorded by readers, a newsagent and one very patient retired teacher.

The 7:40 to the station is late on 62 per cent of days, by four minutes on average. The 7:55, which leaves the depot rather than coming over the ridge, is late on fewer than one day in twenty.

The bus company says it will move the 7:40’s start point from next spring. Until then, our advice is the 7:55.

/news/inside-the-bakery-that-has-opened-.title: Inside the bakery that has opened at 4am every day since 1958

entry.title: Inside the bakery that has opened at 4am every day since 1958

fields.author: Priya Nand
fields.standfirst: Two ovens, one family and a queue that starts before the first bus.
fields.image_alt: Loaves cooling on wooden racks in a bakery before dawn
fields.body:
The lights at Hollins Bakery come on at a quarter to four. By the time the first bus passes at six, there are three hundred loaves on the racks and a queue at the door.

The bakery has opened at four every day since Albert Hollins took over the lease in 1958, Christmas Day included. His granddaughter Jo runs it now, on the same two ovens he installed.

Asked why they have never moved the opening time, Jo Hollins said the night shift at the mill finishes at four. “They were our first customers. They still are.”

seo.description: Two ovens, one family and a queue that starts before the first bus.

/news/the-last-lighthouse-keeper-on-the-.title: The last lighthouse keeper on the east coast hands over the keys

entry.title: The last lighthouse keeper on the east coast hands over the keys

fields.author: Tom Reilly
fields.standfirst: Forty-one years, three storms that made the news and one that did not.
fields.image_alt: The white lighthouse on the point, waves breaking below it
fields.body:
Ellen Marsh climbed the 114 steps of the point lighthouse for the last time on Tuesday morning. The light has been automatic since 1998, but someone still had to keep it, and for forty-one years that was her.

She remembers three storms that made the national news, and one in 1987 that did not, when the lamp failed at two in the morning and she turned it by hand until dawn.

The keys go to the trust that now owns the tower. Marsh is moving to a bungalow inland. “I want to sleep through a gale,” she said.

seo.description: Forty-one years, three storms that made the news and one that did not.

fields.standfirst: From the festival winner opening at the old Regal to two reissues worth the drive, the films to see before the year turns.

fields.body:
The Regal opens this year’s festival winner on the 14th, a quiet film about a lock keeper that won the audience prize as well as the jury’s.

Two restorations are worth the drive to the city: a 1950s thriller with a new score, and a documentary about the last steam trains, shot partly on our own branch line.

/news/why-are-so-many-thai-restaurants-h.title: Why are so many Thai restaurants hidden in London pubs?

entry.title: Why are so many Thai restaurants hidden in London pubs?

fields.author: Mei Lin
fields.standfirst: Behind the bar of a hundred old pubs, a small kitchen turns out some of the city’s best green curry. How a licensing quirk of the 1980s built a tradition.
fields.image_alt: A pub kitchen hatch with a handwritten Thai menu above it
fields.body:
Walk into an old pub in London and there is a good chance the kitchen at the back is Thai. There are more than a hundred of them, and most began the same way.

In the 1980s, landlords who had lost their food trade could let their kitchens to a cook without a second licence. Thai families, many newly arrived, took them on, and the arrangement stuck.

Our travel writer spent a week eating her way round twelve of them. The best green curry, she reports, was served under a dartboard.
